tldr: This paper presents DECOWAM, a new world-action model for whole-body control and future video prediction on quadrupedal mobile manipulators. By explicitly decoupling base velocity, arm motion, and camera ego-motion, it reduces action error by 21.7% with only 25.95M lightweight adaptation parameters, while demonstrating high whole-body coordination and robustness to disturbances in real-robot experiments.
hero_caption: Overall architecture, training, and real-robot deployment pipeline of DECOWAM. (A) Freezing the pretrained backbone (FastWAM), it adds residual adapters, a distilled future bottleneck, adversarial base/arm latent separation, and ego-motion conditioning via base velocity. (B) At inference time, it outputs 14-dimensional actions as a causal model without using future images. (C) It uses a two-stage setup: pre-adaptation to real-robot data (Stage 1) followed by parameter-efficient adaptation (Stage 2).
overview:
Mobile manipulation while on the move, especially with legged robots, is notoriously challenging because it requires coordinating base locomotion and precise arm movements at the same time. World-action models (WAMs), which predict and generate both future visual observations and robot actions jointly, have gained strong attention recently. However, existing models were primarily designed for fixed-base setups. As a result, camera viewpoint changes caused by base motion (ego-motion) get entangled with arm and environmental movements in pixel space, leaving models unable to handle the multi-rate control timescales typical of legged platforms.

To solve this, the authors developed DECOWAM, an embodiment-aware decoupled approach. Specifically, they freeze most of a high-capacity video and action backbone, FastWAM, and introduce dedicated conditioning interfaces that explicitly separate base velocity, arm trajectories, and camera ego-motion. They also built an action-equivalent future bottleneck that distills action-critical features from privileged future video into a causal model (using only observations up to the current step), along with an adversarial learning mechanism that separates base and arm latent representations. Furthermore, they constructed ARMDOG, a high-quality real-robot dataset collected on a wheeled quadruped manipulator with synchronized signals.

On a fixed replay benchmark, DECOWAM reduced action mean squared error (MSE) by 21.7% compared to the base model while improving future video prediction quality. Across 79 real-robot closed-loop trials per system, it achieved task completion rates comparable to or better than state-of-the-art baselines, while setting the highest scores in whole-body coordination and base-displacement robustness. By cleanly separating whole-body roles, DECOWAM clearly shows that efficient, stable whole-body control and environmental prediction can coexist under moving viewpoints.
contributions: Proposed a world-action model framework tailored for legged mobile manipulation that explicitly separates base control, arm motion, and camera ego-motion.
Developed residual adapters and an action-equivalent future bottleneck that achieve highly accurate adaptation with only 25.95M trainable parameters while keeping most backbone weights frozen.
Introduced latent representations that decouple base and arm commands without interference using gradient reversal layers (GRL), alongside base-velocity conditioning for video generation.
Built and released ARMDOG, a real-robot dataset synchronizing video, whole-body state and action, and language instructions at 15 Hz on a quadruped manipulator.

sections.heading: Why are moving viewpoints and whole-body coordination so hard on legged robots?
sections.summary: This section outlines the structural difficulties when transferring vision-language-action (VLA) models and world models from fixed-base setups to legged platforms. To resolve the confusion between camera ego-motion and environmental changes, as well as the mismatch between arm and base control rates, DECOWAM introduces an embodiment-aware factorization approach.
sections.details:
Robots that can move through the real world and perform dexterous manipulation have long been a core goal of robotics and Embodied AI. While recent VLA models (such as Aloha and $\pi_0$) and world-action models have achieved impressive results on fixed-base arms, directly applying them to legged robots runs into three fundamental roadblocks.

First is the dynamic viewpoint. Because the camera is mounted on a swaying base, raw pixel changes blend environmental motion, arm movements, and the camera's own movement (ego-motion) caused by base locomotion. Trying to solve this with a single monolithic video generator makes it very hard to learn appearance changes driven by camera motion correctly.

Second is multi-rate action coupling. Arm joint control requires high-rate, fine-grained adjustments (around 15 to 30 Hz), whereas base velocity commands are sufficient at lower rates (around 3 to 5 Hz). Bundling these into a single uniform action vector makes it extremely difficult to track behaviors operating across different scales using one shared representation.

Third is hierarchical intent. In real-world tasks, navigation (where to move) and manipulation (how to move the arm) alternate continuously.

To overcome these hurdles, the paper proposes DECOWAM, an approach that factorizes where the base moves, how the arm acts, and how camera ego-motion alters future pixels as explicit factors. The authors also collected ARMDOG, a synchronized real-robot dataset to train and evaluate these components.

sections.heading: How it differs from prior work: Moving from fixed bases to a legged whole-body world-action model
sections.summary: Related work is organized across four areas: fixed-base VLA models, world models for robotics, legged mobile manipulation, and robot datasets. The authors point out that no prior legged model had unified video prediction and whole-body action while structurally decoupling ego-motion from actions.
sections.details:
To clarify its positioning, the paper compares DECOWAM with four research directions:

- Fixed-base VLA models:
Strong base policies like OpenVLA, $\pi_0$, and RDT-2 exist, but they essentially regress arm trajectories directly from current observations. They lack structures to explicitly forecast future video developments or disentangle viewpoint shifts caused by base motion from arm movements.

- World models for robot control:
World models that generate future observation video (such as UniSim, X-WAM, and FastWAM) have shown a path to combining visual prediction with action generation. However, existing models pursue scale as general-purpose simulators, leaving embodiment-adaptive structures tailored to legged ego-motion and base/arm decoupling unexplored.

- Mobile manipulation:
Research on wheeled robots and Mobile ALOHA has advanced teleoperation and whole-body policies, but many rely on cascaded pipelines that run navigation and manipulation sequentially. Combining a predictive video generation model with an integrated whole-body policy had no precedent on legged robots.

- Robot datasets:
While large-scale datasets like Open X-Embodiment and DROID exist, datasets where legged base ego-motion streams, manipulator actions, video, and language instructions are strictly time-synchronized as a single unified unit were lacking. ARMDOG fills this gap.

sections.heading: The foundation: FastWAM as a diffusion backbone spinning video and action together
sections.summary: This section briefly describes FastWAM, the baseline architecture behind DECOWAM. It explains how combining the Wan-2.2 video diffusion backbone and an ActionDiT action prediction branch enables simultaneous generation of future video and action chunks from current images, states, and language.
sections.details:
To understand DECOWAM, it helps to review the baseline FastWAM first. FastWAM is a world-action model combining the Wan-2.2 video diffusion backbone with an ActionDiT branch specialized for action prediction. Both branches are trained simultaneously under a shared Continuous Flow Matching framework.

In this robot setup, the model takes a single current RGB image, precomputed language features, and a 14-dimensional state token representing the robot's proprioception. As output, it simultaneously generates 8 future RGB frames and a 48-step chunk of 14-dimensional whole-body actions.

In full fine-tuning of FastWAM, an overwhelming 6020.75M parameters were trained out of a total 6725.44M parameters (around 6.7 billion). Retraining such a massive model from scratch or tuning the entire architecture for every robot task is extremely inefficient. DECOWAM retains this joint prediction framework while upgrading it with four modular, decoupled components.

sections.heading: The core of DECOWAM: Four decoupling mechanisms and staged adaptation
sections.summary: This section details the concrete design and training stages of DECOWAM. Training is split into two stages: in Stage 2, the pretrained model is frozen, and residual adapters, a future bottleneck, adversarial latent separation, and video conditioning via base-velocity tokens are trained using a tiny fraction of parameters.
sections.details:
DECOWAM's technical strength lies in cleanly separating control roles both mathematically and structurally.

### Problem Formulation and Action Vector Decomposition (IV-A)
From language $\ell$, current image $x_0$, and whole-body state $s_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{14}$, the model predicts future video $x_{1:T}$ ($T=8$) and an action chunk $\mathbf{a}_{1:K} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times 14}$ ($K=48$). The 14 dimensions break down into arm and gripper at $[0:7]$, base velocities at $[7:10]$ ($v_x, v_y, \omega_z$), and padding at $[10:14]$. Base velocity serves a dual role: it is a control target to predict and simultaneously a driver that moves the camera and changes future visual observations.

### Staged Parameter Efficiency (IV-B)
Training proceeds in two stages. In Stage 1, the entire FastWAM model is adapted to real-robot data for 50k steps to align domains. In Stage 2, these weights are completely frozen, and only the four added modules (residual adapters, future bottleneck, base/arm decoupling, and ego-motion conditioning) are trained. This slashes trainable parameters from 6020.75M to just 25.95M (a reduction of about 232x). The residual adapters use a compact bottleneck dimension of 128, learning robot-specific corrections without disrupting original video pretraining representations.

### Decoupled Conditioning Interfaces (IV-C)
This is DECOWAM's key novelty:
- Future Information Bottleneck: A privileged Teacher network sees future frames $x_{1:T}$ during training, which is distilled into a causal Student network that only observes the current frame and state. A quotient geometry loss ensures that trajectories with similar actions stay close in latent space, teaching the student only the essential information needed for action execution. At inference time, the teacher is dropped, using only the student feature $z_s$.
- Base and Arm Latent Separation: Action context is projected into separate 16-dimensional base latents $z_{\mathrm{base}}$ and arm latents $z_{\mathrm{arm}}$. A gradient reversal layer (GRL) enforces adversarial learning so that arm actions cannot be predicted from base latents, and base actions cannot be predicted from arm latents, making both spaces independent.
- Ego-Motion-Aware Video Conditioning: The normalized current base velocity vector $v_0$ is linearly projected into an ego-motion token and added to all video tokens. This frees the video generator from having to infer camera motion purely from pixels, allowing it to leverage base velocity directly as a visual viewpoint driver.

### Objectives and Deployment (IV-D)
Both action and video predictions are optimized using Flow Matching losses. At inference, privileged teachers and auxiliary heads are discarded, enabling fast, causal sampling from current observations alone.

captions.F2: Architecture of the action-equivalent future bottleneck. During training, a privileged Teacher ($q_t$) observing future video summaries learns action reconstruction and geometric preservation, distilling that knowledge into a Student ($q_s$) that only sees current observations. At real-robot deployment, only the student branch is retained, preventing future information leakage.

sections.heading: The new ARMDOG dataset: Legs, arm, and viewpoint fully synchronized at 15 Hz
sections.summary: This section introduces ARMDOG, a dataset collected on a real quadruped platform equipped with a 6-DoF arm. Video, whole-body states/actions, and language instructions are strictly aligned at 15 Hz, providing the empirical foundation for training the models in this study.
sections.details:
No matter how clever a model architecture is, it cannot learn without data where whole-body actions, ego-motion, and visual changes on a legged robot are cleanly aligned. The research team built the ARMDOG dataset using a wheeled quadruped robot (16 leg joints, a 6-DoF arm, and a 1-DoF gripper).

Converted from raw HDF5 files, the dataset stores 15 Hz RGB video, 14-dimensional whole-body state/action tensors, natural language task descriptions, and precomputed language embeddings in strict time synchronization.

The quality-filtered corpus comprises 1,487 episodes and 343,550 frames (around 321.3 minutes). Tasks are dominated by bottle pick-and-place (56%) and block placement (39%), with the rest covering general object manipulation (4%) and ramp climbing (1%), balancing manipulation with locomotion.

A carefully selected subset was used for training and evaluation. Stage 2 training used 214 episodes across 26 tasks, while offline replay evaluation was conducted on a fixed Box-val slice of 23 episodes (4,323 frames) across 8 tasks.

captions.F3: ARMDOG dataset composition and model interface. (a) Task distribution shows bottle and block pick-and-place tasks account for about 95%. (b) Overall dataset scale comprises 1,487 episodes and roughly 343.5k frames. (c) Explicit mapping from inputs (text, current RGB, state) to outputs (future RGB, 14D actions).

sections.heading: Experimental results: Stronger offline prediction and superior whole-body coordination on the robot
sections.summary: The authors evaluated DECOWAM through offline replay benchmarks, ablation studies, comparisons with other VLA/WAM models, and 79 closed-loop real-robot trials per method. DECOWAM cut action error by 21.7% and eliminated unnecessary base jitter on the real robot, achieving superior coordination and robustness.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted in four phases: offline prediction benchmarks, internal ablations, comparisons with other methods, and real-robot deployment.

### Offline Replay Evaluation and Ablations (VI-B)
On the fixed 23-episode validation slice, DECOWAM reduced video frame MSE by 15.03% and action MSE by 21.71% compared to the FastWAM 50k-step baseline. PSNR also improved by 0.222 dB.
Ablation experiments showed that removing either the future bottleneck or ego-motion conditioning caused clear drops in both video and action accuracy. This demonstrates that performance gains stem from the decoupling mechanisms themselves, not just from adding residual adapters.

### Comparison with Other VLAs and World Models
Compared to action-only VLA models (such as X-VLA and $\pi_{0.5}$), DECOWAM maintained strong performance—improving action MSE by 69.9% over $\pi_{0.5}$, though falling slightly behind specialized X-VLA on pure action error. Crucially, while VLAs only output actions, DECOWAM concurrently predicts 8 future video frames. Against existing world-action models (WAMs) like Motus and X-WAM, DECOWAM took first place across all video and action metrics.

### Closed-Loop Deployment on Real Robots (VI-C)
In extensive closed-loop testing on the physical quadruped manipulator across 79 trials per method, DECOWAM achieved a 58.2% (46/79) overall success rate with an average completion time of 49 seconds. This was 16 seconds faster than FastWAM (57.0%, 65 s) and dramatically outperformed X-WAM (15.2%, 82 s).
Looking closer at whole-body coordination success rate (WBCM-SR) and base-displacement robustness (BDP-SR), DECOWAM outperformed FastWAM by 10.1 percentage points on coordination and 17.7 percentage points on displacement robustness.
A clear qualitative difference emerged when reaching for objects on a table: baseline methods (X-VLA and FastWAM) suffered from unnecessary base jitter due to locomotion bias in the data, leading to failures. In contrast, DECOWAM held the base completely stationary while accurately extending only the arm to complete grasps.

### Parameter Efficiency and Inference Speed (VI-D)
While Stage 2 trains only 25.95M parameters—roughly 232x fewer than FastWAM—inference latency increased by only 11.4% (from 208.5 ms to 232.3 ms).

captions.F5: Comparison of whole-body coordination on the physical quadruped manipulator. When reaching for a tabletop object, X-VLA (top) and FastWAM (middle) move the base unnecessarily when it should stay still, causing grasp failures. In contrast, DECOWAM (bottom) keeps the base stably anchored while accurately extending the arm, successfully grasping the target.

sections.heading: Conclusion: How embodiment-aware factorization opens new possibilities for legged robots
sections.summary: This section summarizes the achievements of DECOWAM. It concludes that explicitly separating base motion, arm control, and ego-motion enables parameter-efficient learning alongside sophisticated whole-body coordination on physical robots.
sections.details:
This paper introduced DECOWAM, a world-action model tailored for legged mobile manipulators. Rather than training the entire network end-to-end indiscriminately, the work highlights the importance of embedding physical robot morphology—how the body is structured, where cameras sit, and how they move—into network design and loss formulations.

By tuning just 25.95M parameters in Stage 2, DECOWAM substantially boosted backbone prediction quality and enabled smooth, jitter-free whole-body coordination on real hardware. This offers a highly practical and valuable design blueprint for deploying future Embodied AI and world models on physical robots.

takeaways: For robots with moving cameras, explicitly feeding base velocity (ego-motion) as a conditioning token to the video generator is far more effective than forcing it to infer camera movement purely from pixels.
In whole-body control, enforcing latent independence between base (navigation) and arm (manipulation) spaces using gradient reversal layers prevents mutual interference and erratic base jitter.
An action-equivalent future bottleneck that distills essential control representations from privileged future video during training serves as a powerful guide for parameter-efficient adaptation.

Rather than retraining massive pretrained video-action backbones end-to-end, adding compact adapters with embodiment-aware interfaces preserves general representations while substantially boosting control accuracy.
limitations: Inference latency is around 232 ms (roughly 4.3 Hz), which requires further acceleration or architectural adjustments for high-frequency (30 Hz+) real-time arm trajectory corrections.

The ARMDOG dataset is heavily concentrated on pick-and-place tasks (about 95%), leaving generalizability to rough-terrain locomotion and dynamic obstacle avoidance in mobile manipulation insufficiently explored.
In physical robot testing, the overall task completion rate remained around 58%, showing there is still room for improvement in long-horizon autonomous error recovery.
